source.title: System image
source.note: Source text is authoritative for this transformation; no outside correction or enrichment was applied.

nodes.label: System image
nodes.description: Serialized copy of the entire state of a computer system stored in non-volatile form.

nodes.label: System image vs process image
nodes.description: System image covers entire computer-system state; process image covers a given process state.

nodes.label: Disk clone vs complete system image
nodes.description: Disk cloning is complete only if all relevant state is on disk and accessible.

nodes.label: Persistent vs volatile state
nodes.description: Images make otherwise volatile execution state recoverable.

nodes.label: Hibernation vs backup
nodes.description: Hibernation is a specific RAM-state persistence operation; backup is a broader purpose.

nodes.label: Savestate vs backup
nodes.description: Savestate preserves emulated execution state; the source does not equate it with general backup.

nodes.label: Migration vs restoration
nodes.description: Migration transfers state to another machine; restoration reconstructs prior state.

nodes.label: Lisp image vs database dump
nodes.description: Both persist state, but Lisp images can combine executable code and application data.

nodes.label: World vs incremental World
nodes.description: Full World contains OS/apps/data; incremental World contains changes from a base.

nodes.label: System image vs core dump
nodes.description: Similar structure does not imply identical purpose.

nodes.label: Image vs source code
nodes.description: An image may contain compiled/customized runtime state rather than source text.

nodes.label: Image distribution vs rebuild
nodes.description: Distribution of initialized images avoids repeated startup initialization.

nodes.label: Runtime state vs program artifact
nodes.description: Image can combine executable code, application data, and runtime state.

nodes.label: System image restoration
nodes.description: system_state → serialize → persistent_image → deserialize → prior_state

nodes.label: Disk completeness
nodes.description: complete_image ≈ disk_image only_if all_relevant_state ∈ disk

nodes.label: Process persistence
nodes.description: process_state(t0) → process_image → later_restore → process_state(t0)

nodes.label: Hibernation
nodes.description: RAM_state → persistent_image → power_saving → restore

nodes.label: DBMS persistence
nodes.description: database_state → database_dump → shutdown → restart → intact_state

nodes.label: Emulator savestate
nodes.description: emulated_state → savestate → load → prior_state

nodes.label: Mobile-agent migration
nodes.description: agent_state → save → copy → restart_on_destination

nodes.label: Lisp image
nodes.description: running_Lisp + compiled_code + data → dump → executable_image

nodes.label: Incremental World
nodes.description: base_World + delta → reconstructed_World

nodes.label: Image/core-dump distinction
nodes.description: structural_similarity ≠ identical_purpose

nodes.label: Definition
nodes.description: System image is a serialized copy of entire computer-system state in non-volatile form.

nodes.label: Disk completeness
nodes.description: Disk cloning can produce a system image only when relevant state is on disk; some state may be outside disks or inaccessible.

nodes.label: Backup
nodes.description: Exact shutdown/restoration capability makes system images usable as backups.

nodes.label: Hibernation
nodes.description: Hibernation images the computer's entire RAM.

nodes.label: Process image
nodes.description: Process image captures process state and creates persistence.

nodes.label: DBMS
nodes.description: DBMS can dump database state before closing and restore it after restart.

nodes.label: Emulator
nodes.description: Emulators may save system images called savestates in video gaming.

nodes.label: Code mobility
nodes.description: Mobile agents can migrate by saving, copying, and restarting state elsewhere.

nodes.label: Language support
nodes.description: Smalltalk and Lisp support system images; Lisp can preserve compiled/customized code and loaded data.

nodes.label: Distribution
nodes.description: Executable images can be distributed to avoid repeated initialization.

nodes.label: Lisp Worlds
nodes.description: Lisp Machines boot from Worlds containing OS, applications, and data; incremental Worlds store changes.

nodes.label: Core dumps
nodes.description: System images resemble core dumps structurally but have different purposes.

nodes.label: A disk clone is always a complete system image
nodes.description: False: non-disk state and privilege limits can make it incomplete.

nodes.label: System image means disk image
nodes.description: False: disk is only one possible state substrate.

nodes.label: Process image means the whole machine
nodes.description: False: it captures one process.

nodes.label: Hibernation only saves files
nodes.description: False: the source says the entire RAM is imaged.

nodes.label: Savestate is source code
nodes.description: False: it is saved emulated execution state.

nodes.label: Migration is only copying
nodes.description: False: the source includes restarting on the destination.

nodes.label: Lisp image contains only code
nodes.description: False: it can contain compiled code and application data.

nodes.label: Incremental World is a full independent World
nodes.description: False: it contains changes from a base.

nodes.label: Core dump and system image have same purpose
nodes.description: False: the source explicitly distinguishes purpose.

source_claims.text: System image is a serialized copy of entire computer-system state in non-volatile form.
Disk cloning can produce a system image only when relevant state is on disk; some state may be outside disks or inaccessible.
Exact shutdown/restoration capability makes system images usable as backups.
Hibernation images the computer's entire RAM.
Process image captures process state and creates persistence.
DBMS can dump database state before closing and restore it after restart.
Emulators may save system images called savestates in video gaming.
Mobile agents can migrate by saving, copying, and restarting state elsewhere.
Smalltalk and Lisp support system images; Lisp can preserve compiled/customized code and loaded data.
Executable images can be distributed to avoid repeated initialization.
Lisp Machines boot from Worlds containing OS, applications, and data; incremental Worlds store changes.
System images resemble core dumps structurally but have different purposes.
